episode_thesis: Kaminski and Kaastrup-Larsen argue that return dispersion among trend followers is not random but the fingerprint of design choices (speed, asset-class allocation, alternative markets, carry), none of which dominates every year, so an investor cannot pick a winning factor and should hold two or three different CTAs. They add that the recent underperformance of alternative-market trend is a regime/sector effect (gas and power, credit after the COVID and Ukraine shocks), that alternative markets are a diversification argument rather than a better-trend argument, and that turbulence can be split into magnitude surprises (bad for CTAs) and correlation surprises (inflection points that drive dispersion).

speakers.name: Katy Kaminski
speakers.role: Systematic researcher at AlphaSimplex; co-author (with Alex Greyserman) of a book on trend following; former CTA allocator
speakers.speaker_note: Name spelled Katie Kaminsky in captions. Two ledger claims carry corrections: MT220-C03-1 (surprise scenarios: more cuts than expected or no cut would be the shock; a 50bp cut is what was expected) and MT220-C11-1 (Liberation Day is not in the turbulence data set; she only presumes it is a magnitude surprise). Both are cited under the corrected reading.

worldview_premises.premise: Return dispersion among trend managers follows from design choices (speed, asset allocation, alternative markets, carry) and from basic math of differing volatilities and correlations, so it is explainable and can be estimated theoretically.
worldview_premises.support: Man AHL 'Dynamics of dispersion', her book chapter 11, and treating managers as random variables.

worldview_premises.premise: No single design factor is the main driver of dispersion; each dominates in a different year (fixed income in 2019, no equities in 2025), and no style factor persists.
worldview_premises.support: Her style-factor tracking at AlphaSimplex and the Man paper's yearly results.

worldview_premises.premise: Faster trend following gives more crisis protection; the industry has drifted to slower products, so replicators and slow managers get less crisis alpha even though slow did better recently.
worldview_premises.support: Man AHL paper and her 'CTA style evolution' study; history of the CTA index.

worldview_premises.premise: CTA indices are not investable and managers' styles drift, so one buys today's managers, not the index; study aspects of managers (speed, markets) rather than index behaviour.
A trend follower should include every asset, since assets that never trended (metals, palladium, copper, platinum) can start to trend.
worldview_premises.support: Past debates over excluding metals; recent trends in platinum, palladium, gold, nickel, copper.

worldview_premises.premise: Adding low-correlation trend P&L streams raises portfolio Sharpe mathematically; alternative markets provide this diversification, but higher costs offset some of the Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Portfolio-theory argument in the Quantica paper and her own book.

worldview_premises.premise: Extreme outperformance of alternative markets in 2020-22 came from specific sectors (gas and power, credit), raising expectations, which is why three weaker years caused doubt; those assets have been range-bound since the shocks.
worldview_premises.support: Quantica's 50 traditional versus 120 alternative market comparison.

worldview_premises.premise: Crowding is two-edged for trend: it still works in crowded liquid markets, but capacity-limited markets may have looked better in backtests when fewer participants traded them.
worldview_premises.support: No study; she wants a case-study analysis.

worldview_premises.premise: Macro and systematic macro outperformed trend around Liberation Day, which motivates research on economic versus technical trends.
worldview_premises.support: Observed April 2025 results; paper in progress.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why fixed income trend signals have not built despite many themes

steps.from: Market already prices Fed cuts (SOFR near 3.4% versus fed funds at 4.25-4.5%)
steps.to: Bond trend signals stay mixed and weak, teetering between long and short
steps.why: The market has been anticipating the Fed, so no sustained one-way move.

steps.from: Outcome that differs from pricing (far more cuts than expected, or no cut)
steps.to: A large move and a trend catalyst
steps.why: Only a surprise relative to pricing moves a priced market; a 50bp cut is what was expected.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Mixed signals in September 2025: slightly more long in the US, short in the UK and some European bonds; recent jobs data had already priced in cuts.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If futures price future rather than current rates, long yields can rise after cuts (host's point), so direction is not obvious.

mechanism_chains.topic: How design choices become return dispersion across trend managers

steps.from: Speed, allocation, alternative markets, carry differ across managers
steps.to: Different return streams with different vol and correlation
steps.why: Managers as random variables; range of differences set by volatility and correlation.

steps.from: A year with a particular sector trend (2019 fixed income; 2025 no equities in ETFs) or a high-volatility year (2008, 2022)
steps.to: A given factor dominates and the dispersion widens
Much of the dispersion versus the index disappears, but 3-4% remains
steps.why: Residual tracking is normal even for replication (500-600bp slippage).

mechanism_chains.evidence: Man AHL hypothetical-manager aggregation, her chapter 11 random-sampling study, and a random-signal experiment.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; she stresses that no factor is persistent.

steps.to: Point-in-time measure of movement with no data window
steps.why: Correlation needs a window and averages away a one-day event.

steps.from: Decompose into magnitude surprise and correlation surprise
steps.to: Magnitude surprises (Brexit, SVB, Black Friday) hurt CTAs; correlation surprises are inflection points where trend signals rotate and drive dispersion
steps.why: Shock versus change in how managers behave relative to each other.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Her paper 'Quantifying turbulence in CTAs'; plotted history of surprises.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Liberation Day is outside the sample and only presumed to be a magnitude surprise.

mechanism_chains.topic: Alternative markets: why they underperformed recently and what remains

steps.to: Gas and power, credit and similar sectors trended extremely, 40-50% of the outperformance coming from gas and power
steps.why: Specific sector events, not structural better trending.

steps.to: Alternative-market managers lagged for about three years
steps.why: Regime effect, not proof the thesis is broken.

steps.to: Possible crowding and higher transaction costs
steps.why: Host's hypothesis; she wants a case-study test.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Quantica Q3 2025 paper; Sharpe per market adjusted for the period instead of reading which sectors won; only about 10 years of history for such managers.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Costs of exotic contracts reduce the net Sharpe; the benefit is diversification, not better trend.

decision_process.practice: Start simple: pick two or three CTAs that are different, avoid analysis paralysis, combine a faster manager (crisis alpha) with a slower manager or replication product.
decision_process.why: CTAs are among the few alternatives without hidden equity beta; no style factor persists; too much analysis creates false expectations.

decision_process.practice: Track style factors for trend (speed, market size, correlated markets) and regress manager returns to explain relative performance, as equity style factors do.
decision_process.why: Disentangles benchmark from style tilts, year by year.

decision_process.practice: Study hypothetical trend managers built with many designs and aggregated over time rather than a single backtest; use random-signal experiments to split allocation from signal effects.
decision_process.why: Avoid cherry-picking the best backtest version.

decision_process.practice: Do not match absolute Sharpe of an index replication; focus on relative and conditional differences.
decision_process.why: Backtest Sharpe 0.75 versus actual 0.36 reflects that longer lookbacks did better and managers differ.

decision_process.practice: Include all assets in a trend programme, accounting for costs of exotic contracts.
decision_process.why: Non-trending assets can start to trend; diversification raises Sharpe.

decision_process.practice: Evaluate alternative markets by Sharpe per market adjusted for the period and portfolio theory, not by recent sector winners.
Do not read a 400-500bp gap versus the index with two or three CTAs as poor selection.
decision_process.why: Such gaps arise by chance with these correlations.

speakers.evidence_style: Academic literature and her own studies (book chapter 11, CTA style evolution, turbulence paper), mathematical arguments about variance and diversification, and random-sampling or hypothetical-manager simulations; explicit about the short sample for alternative markets.

current_views.view: US fixed income trend signals have barely moved despite many themes (Fed independence, inflation); a bond breakout could be the next trend catalyst.
current_views.reasoning: Many calls from clients and press on fixed income while signals stay put.

current_views.view: Bond market already prices cuts; surprise is needed (more cuts than expected or no cut) for a trend.
current_views.reasoning: SOFR near 3.4%; jobs data baked in.

current_views.view: Systematic macro did better than trend around Liberation Day; researching economic versus technical trends.
In 2025 CTA ETFs that did not trade equities did relatively well.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Inflows into less-liquid markets may have crowded them and added costs, contributing to underperformance.

positions.speaker: Katy Kaminski
positions.position: Mostly a regime effect: the assets that drove 2020-22 gains went range-bound; crowding is two-edged and untested, so she would like a case study.

disagreements.topic: How much an index (or replication) says about manager risk

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Index dispersion depends on constituents; do not conclude replication is better without understanding where dispersion comes from.

positions.speaker: Katy Kaminski
positions.position: The index is not investable and managers drift; replication Sharpe differs from actual; look at relative and conditional differences.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Ledger claim MT220-C03-1 as originally worded had the surprise scenario wrong; the corrected reading (no cut or far more cuts than expected as the shock; a 50bp cut being expected) is used in the map.
Liberation Day is described as a magnitude surprise although it is outside the paper's sample; Kaminski says only that she is 'pretty sure'.
The causal claim that crowding explains recent alternative-market underperformance is untested; both speakers say so.
Alternative-market managers have only about 10 years of history, so conclusions about their long-run Sharpe are weak.
The replication Sharpe gap (0.75 backtest versus 0.36 actual) is explained by lookbacks and manager differences without a quantitative decomposition.
The statement that managers in the Man AHL index have dispersion explained by design and the statement that no factor is the main driver leave open how much dispersion is explained at all.
Alternative-market performance claim: 40-50% from gas and power is from the host's memory.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Speakers point to: the Fed decision relative to pricing (a no-cut or much larger cut would be the catalyst for a bond trend), UK and French budget politics for yields, whether gas and power or credit leave their range, and crowding in less-liquid markets. Horizon: the next Fed meeting for bonds; years for the alternative-market diversification argument.
reader_inferences: (reader) Kaminski's advice to hold two or three different CTAs follows from her finding that no style factor persists and that 3-4% tracking vs the index always remains.
(reader) The magnitude/correlation decomposition suggests a manager-level early-warning measure: rising correlation surprise marks regime rotation, rising magnitude surprise marks shock risk.
(reader) Alternative markets are defended as diversifiers, not as better trend, so their case does not depend on the 2020-22 outperformance.
